title: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
summary: Why one Euler step from noise fails, how a consistency model maps any point of a probability-flow ODE trajectory to its origin, how it is trained by distillation or from scratch, and what one or two steps buy.
outcomes: Explain why a single ODE solver step from pure noise collapses to the data mean
State the self-consistency property and the boundary condition f(x, eps) = x
Compute c_skip and c_out at any noise level and explain why they enforce the boundary
Contrast consistency distillation and consistency training, including the role of the EMA target
Compare consistency models with progressive, adversarial and distribution-matching distillation

lessons.title: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean

blocks.md: From the flow matching course you know the recipe: a network predicts a velocity field, and sampling integrates the ODE $dx/dt = v(x, t)$ from noise to data with many small Euler steps. Each step is one full network evaluation (one **NFE**, number of function evaluations). Diffusion models sample the same way through the **probability flow ODE** (PF ODE), a deterministic ODE whose solutions, started from noise, land on data.

The cost is the number of steps. Song et al. note that iterative diffusion sampling typically needs 10 to 2000 times more compute than single-step generators such as GANs. The EDM sampler (Karras et al.) that consistency models are built on uses 35 NFE on CIFAR-10 and 79 on ImageNet 64x64. Real-time image generation needs one to four.

To see why you cannot just take bigger steps, we use a toy that has an exact answer. The data is one number drawn from a Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma_d = 0.5$ (the same $\sigma_{data} = 0.5$ the papers use for images scaled to [-1, 1]). Noise is added as in EDM: $x_t = x_0 + t\,z$ with $z \sim N(0,1)$, so $x_t$ has variance $\sigma_d^2 + t^2$. Time runs from $\epsilon = 0.002$ to $T = 80$, the values used by Song et al.

blocks.caption: The PF ODE with EDM settings (score of a Gaussian is $-x/(\sigma_d^2+t^2)$) and its closed-form solution. Each trajectory just stretches its starting value.

scenes.caption: Read time right to left for sampling: start at a noisy value and follow the curve down to t = 0.002. Trajectories never cross, so each noisy point has exactly one origin.
The marked points all lie on the trajectory with origin 0.3: x = 0.4243 at t = 0.5, 0.6708 at t = 1, 1.2369 at t = 2 (and 48.0 at t = 80). Every one of them should be mapped back to 0.3.
Move the slider: a different origin gives a different curve. At t = 80 the origin 1.0 sits at 160.0, so the sampler must shrink the noise by a factor of 160 along a curved path.

blocks.prompt: Start from $x_T \sim N(0, 80^2)$ and take one single Euler step of the exact PF ODE from $t = 80$ down to $t = 0.002$. The true samples should have standard deviation 0.5. What standard deviation do the one-step samples have?
blocks.reveal: About **0.0051**. The Euler step uses the slope at $t = 80$, where $dx/dt \approx x/80$, and extrapolates that straight line all the way down. The result is close to the posterior mean $E[x_0 \mid x_T]$ (an Euler step all the way to $t = 0$ lands exactly on it, std 0.0031), which is near 0 for every input: all samples collapse to the data mean. With 2 steps the spread is 0.098, with 10 steps 0.376, and even 50 Euler steps give 0.472 (computed with numpy on the EDM time grid, rho = 7).

blocks.title: Std of samples: Euler steps on the exact PF ODE

scenes.caption: Target: data has standard deviation 0.5. One Euler step gives 0.0051, so every sample is nearly the mean. The ODE is exact here; the only error is discretization.
Simplified: real images have curved, crossing-free but highly nonlinear trajectories, so errors are worse. The point is the same: few steps of a local solver cannot follow a curved path.

blocks.md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

blocks.question: Why do one-step samples from a single Euler step at t = 80 all look like the dataset average, even with a perfect score model?
options: The score model is undertrained at high noise levels
One Euler step extrapolates the slope at t = 80 in a straight line, which lands near the posterior mean instead of following the curved trajectory
The initial noise has too small a variance
Euler steps are stochastic and average out the samples
blocks.explain: In the toy the score is exact, yet one step gives std 0.0051. The error is pure discretization: the straight-line step from t = 80 ends near $E[x_0 \mid x_T]$, which is close to the mean for any input. Euler on the PF ODE is deterministic, and the initial noise is correctly N(0, 80^2).

lessons.title: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin

blocks.md: Song, Dhariwal, Chen and Sutskever (2023) define the **consistency function** of a PF ODE: for any point $(x_t, t)$ on a solution trajectory, $f(x_t, t) = x_\epsilon$, the trajectory's origin at the smallest time $\epsilon$. A **consistency model** $f_\theta$ is a network trained to approximate it.

blocks.tex: f(x_t, t) = f(x_{t'}, t') \quad \text{for all } t, t' \in [\epsilon, T] \text{ on the same trajectory}
blocks.caption: Self-consistency: outputs agree for every pair of points on one trajectory. This is the property the training losses enforce.
Boundary condition: at the smallest time the function is the identity. Every consistency model must satisfy it.

blocks.md: In the toy, the consistency function is available in closed form by inverting the trajectory: $f(x, t) = x\sqrt{(\sigma_d^2 + \epsilon^2)/(\sigma_d^2 + t^2)}$. Sampling is then one evaluation: draw $x_T \sim N(0, T^2)$ and output $f(x_T, T)$. With the exact $f$, the one-step samples have standard deviation 0.499994, matching the target 0.500004 (the std of $x_\epsilon$) to five decimals; the tiny gap comes from drawing $x_T$ from $N(0, T^2)$ instead of the exact $N(0, \sigma_d^2 + T^2)$.

blocks.title: Points on one trajectory all map to the same origin

scenes.caption: Four points on the trajectory whose origin is 0.3, at times 0.1, 1, 10 and 80. They look nothing alike: 48.0 at t = 80 is almost pure noise.
Apply the consistency function to each point. All four outputs are 0.3, the shared origin. That agreement is self-consistency.
One-step sampling only uses the last column: a single evaluation at t = 80 turns noise 48.0 into the data point 0.3.

blocks.md: Compare this with the **denoiser** a diffusion model learns, $D(x, t) \approx E[x_0 \mid x_t]$. For the toy, $D(x, t) = x\,\sigma_d^2/(\sigma_d^2 + t^2)$. At $t = 80$ that gain is 0.00004, so denoised samples have std 0.0031: the mean again. The consistency gain at $t = 80$ is 0.00625, about 160 times larger, because it returns one specific sample instead of the average of all plausible ones.

blocks.title: Gain applied to x: denoiser vs consistency function

scenes.caption: The consistency gain starts at 1 near t = 0.002 (so does the denoiser gain, shown next): with almost no noise, the input is already the answer.

The denoiser (posterior mean) shrinks much faster: 0.5 vs 0.707 at t = 0.5, 0.0099 vs 0.0995 at t = 5. The denoiser averages over all origins; the consistency function picks the one on this trajectory.

blocks.md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain regression to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

blocks.question: A colleague trains a network to predict the clean image from pure noise with an L2 loss on (noise, random training image) pairs, and calls it a one-step consistency model. What will its samples look like?
options: Sharp and diverse, identical to a consistency model
Pure noise, because the input has no information
A blurry average image, because L2 regression on random pairs learns the conditional mean
Exact copies of training images
blocks.explain: Random pairs carry no link between a given noise and a given image, so the L2-optimal output is the average of all images, like the denoiser gain 0.00004 in the toy. A consistency model is trained on pairs that lie on the same ODE trajectory, which defines a deterministic noise-to-data map.

lessons.title: The boundary condition and the c_skip, c_out parameterization

blocks.md: The boundary condition $f(x, \epsilon) = x$ is what makes training work: without it, the constant function $f \equiv 0$ is perfectly self-consistent and would be a trivial minimizer. Song et al. call it the most confining architectural constraint and enforce it with skip connections, borrowing the EDM network design:

blocks.tex: f_\theta(x, t) = c_{skip}(t)\,x + c_{out}(t)\,F_\theta(x, t), \qquad c_{skip}(\epsilon) = 1,\; c_{out}(\epsilon) = 0
blocks.caption: $F_\theta$ is any free-form network with output the same shape as $x$. At $t = \epsilon$ the network's output is multiplied by zero, so the boundary condition holds for every $\theta$.

blocks.md: EDM uses $c_{skip}(t) = \sigma_d^2/(t^2 + \sigma_d^2)$ and $c_{out}(t) = \sigma_d t/\sqrt{\sigma_d^2 + t^2}$. At $t = \epsilon = 0.002$ these give 0.999984 and 0.002, close to but not exactly 1 and 0. Song et al. (Appendix C) shift time by $\epsilon$ so the boundary holds exactly:

blocks.caption: The consistency model parameterization used in all experiments of Song et al. (2023).

blocks.title: c_skip and c_out at several noise levels (sigma_d = 0.5, eps = 0.002)

scenes.caption: Low noise (left): c_skip is 1 and c_out is 0, so the output is the input itself. At t = 0.002 exactly, the network cannot change anything.
High noise (right): c_skip falls to 0.0099 at t = 5 and below 0.0001 at t = 80, while c_out rises to 0.5 = sigma_d. The output is almost entirely the network's prediction, scaled to the data's std.

Bottom row: what F must output (as a multiple of x) for f to equal the toy's exact consistency function, from F = (f - c_skip x)/c_out. All values stay small (at most 0.58): the scalings keep F's job well conditioned at every t.

blocks.title: c_skip and c_out across all noise levels

scenes.caption: The curves cross at about t = 0.63, just above sigma_d = 0.5 (at t = 0.5, c_skip is 0.502 and c_out 0.352). Below it the model mostly passes x through; above it the network does most of the work.

blocks.prompt: Suppose an untrained $F_\theta$ outputs random garbage. What does the consistency model output at $t = 0.002$, and at $t = 80$?
blocks.reveal: At $t = 0.002$ it outputs exactly $x$, because $c_{out} = 0$ and $c_{skip} = 1$: the boundary condition holds from step zero of training, garbage or not. At $t = 80$ it outputs about $0.5 \times$ garbage, since $c_{skip} < 0.0001$ there. Training propagates correctness outward from the boundary, which is why low noise levels are learned first and errors accumulate as $t$ grows.

blocks.md: Later work kept the idea but simplified the coefficients. In **TrigFlow** (Lu and Song, 2024) noise is mixed as $x_t = \cos(t)\,x_0 + \sin(t)\,z$ with $z \sim N(0, \sigma_d^2 I)$ for $t \in [0, \pi/2]$, and the consistency model is $f_\theta(x_t, t) = \cos(t)\,x_t - \sin(t)\,\sigma_d F_\theta(x_t/\sigma_d, t)$, so $c_{skip} = \cos t$ and $c_{out} = -\sigma_d \sin t$. Both equal the boundary values 1 and 0 at $t = 0$. The paper notes TrigFlow is a special case of flow matching, the formulation from the previous course.

blocks.question: A teammate drops c_skip and c_out and uses f(x, t) = F(x, t) directly, trained with the consistency loss only. What is the main risk?
options: Training becomes slower but converges to the same solution
Nothing ties the outputs to data, so a constant output such as f = 0 minimizes the loss
The model can no longer be sampled in one step
The ODE solver in the teacher becomes unstable
blocks.explain: Self-consistency only says outputs agree along a trajectory; a constant function agrees everywhere. The boundary condition f(x, eps) = x anchors the chain to real data, and the paper states it precludes the trivial solution. (Song et al. also allow a piecewise version that returns x at t = eps, but some anchor is required.)

lessons.title: Training: consistency distillation, consistency training, EMA

blocks.md: We cannot compute the true consistency function for images, so training enforces self-consistency between **adjacent** times. Discretize $[\epsilon, T]$ into $N$ points $t_1 = \epsilon < t_2 < \dots < t_N = T$ using the EDM grid $t_i = (\epsilon^{1/\rho} + \tfrac{i-1}{N-1}(T^{1/\rho} - \epsilon^{1/\rho}))^\rho$ with $\rho = 7$. With $N = 18$ the grid is 0.002, 0.0075, 0.0229, 0.0599, 0.1395, 0.2964, 0.5853, 1.0882, ..., 80: dense at low noise, sparse at high noise.

**Consistency distillation (CD)** uses a pretrained diffusion model (the teacher score $s_\phi$). Take a data point $x$, add noise to get $x_{t_{n+1}} = x + t_{n+1} z$, run *one* ODE solver step with the teacher to get $\hat{x}_{t_n}$, then pull the two model outputs together:

blocks.caption: $f_\theta$ is the online network (gets gradients). $f_{\theta^-}$ is the target network, an exponential moving average (EMA) of past $\theta$ with no gradient. $d$ is a distance: L2, L1 or LPIPS in the paper; $\lambda \equiv 1$ worked well.

nodes.label:
x at t_n+1
x + t_n+1 z

scenes.caption: Sample a data point and a step index n, then noise it to time t_n+1 (the noisier of the two adjacent times).
The online network maps the noisy point to its estimate of the origin.
The frozen teacher moves the same point one ODE step down to t_n. This is the only place the diffusion model is used: one step, not a full sample.
The target network maps the less noisy point to its origin. Both points lie (approximately) on one trajectory, so both outputs should agree.
The loss pulls the online output toward the target. Gradients flow only into theta; the target is then updated as an EMA of theta.

blocks.title: One CD step on the toy, numbers from numpy
blocks.code:
x = sample_data()                 # data point
n = 6                             # t_8, t_7 in 1-based notation
t_hi, t_lo = t[n + 1], t[n]
z = randn()
x_hi = x + t_hi * z
score = teacher(x_hi, t_hi)       # frozen diffusion model
x_lo = x_hi - (t_lo - t_hi) * t_hi * score   # one Euler step
out = f(theta, x_hi, t_hi)
tgt = f(theta_ema, x_lo, t_lo)    # no gradient
loss = (out - tgt) ** 2
theta = theta - lr * grad(loss)
theta_ema = mu * theta_ema + (1 - mu) * theta

scenes.caption: Draw a data point and an adjacent pair of grid times from the N = 18 EDM grid.
Noise the data to the higher time. In the toy the teacher score is exact: -x/(0.25 + t^2).
One Euler step down to t_lo gives 0.7239. The true trajectory through 1.1705 passes 0.7525 at t_lo: the solver step has error.
Plug in the exact consistency function as both networks. The two outputs still differ (0.4887 vs 0.4702) because x_lo is off the trajectory.
So the zero-loss solution of discrete CD is not the exact consistency function: it inherits the teacher solver's error, which Theorem 1 bounds by O(dt^p) for a p-th order solver.

blocks.md: How large is that inherited error? In the toy everything is linear, so we can solve for the model that makes the CD loss exactly zero on the N-point grid (a chain of per-step gains starting from 1 at $\epsilon$) and sample from it in one step. The result depends on the teacher's solver and on $N$, exactly as Theorem 1 predicts.

blocks.title: One-step sample std of the zero-loss CD model (target 0.5)

scenes.caption: With N = 18 and an Euler teacher the distilled model under-spreads samples by 15% (std 0.4230). A second-order Heun teacher cuts the error to 5.5% (0.5276).
More grid points shrink both errors (N = 80: 0.4823 and 0.5012). Song et al. found Heun with N = 18 best on CIFAR-10, and CD quality insensitive to N once N is large enough.

blocks.md: **Consistency training (CT)** drops the teacher. Song et al. use the unbiased estimator $\nabla \log p_t(x_t) = -E[(x_t - x)/t^2 \mid x_t]$: given the clean $x$ that produced $x_t$, the score is estimated by $-(x_t - x)/t^2$. Plug that into the Euler step and something neat happens: $\hat{x}_{t_n}$ becomes exactly $x + t_n z$, the same data point noised with the **same** $z$ at the lower level.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{CT} = \mathbb{E}\big[\lambda(t_n)\, d\big(f_\theta(x + t_{n+1} z,\, t_{n+1}),\; f_{\theta^-}(x + t_n z,\, t_n)\big)\big]
blocks.caption: No diffusion model anywhere. In the toy example, the CT pair is (1.1705, 0.7683) versus the CD pair (1.1705, 0.7239); the true trajectory point is 0.7525.

blocks.md: The single-sample estimate is noisy, so CT has more variance than CD. Theorem 2 shows the two losses agree up to $o(\Delta t)$ as the grid gets finer, so CT uses a curriculum that grows $N$ during training (from $s_0 = 2$ to $s_1 = 150$ on CIFAR-10): small $N$ means faster, more biased learning early, large $N$ means less bias at the end.

About the EMA target: Song et al. found $\theta^- \leftarrow \mu\theta^- + (1-\mu)\theta$ with stopgrad stabilizes training, like target networks in deep RL. Their CIFAR-10 CD run used $\mu = 0$ and ImageNet used 0.95. Song and Dhariwal (2023) later argued the teacher EMA should be **zero** for CT (an earlier theoretical argument was flawed) and removing it notably improved FID.

blocks.question: You have no pretrained diffusion model and a large image dataset. Which method can you use, and what replaces the teacher?
options: Consistency distillation, with the online network acting as the teacher
Neither: consistency models always need a pretrained diffusion model
Progressive distillation, starting from a random teacher
Consistency training, where the score is estimated from the known clean image as -(x_t - x)/t^2, giving the pair x + t_n+1 z and x + t_n z
blocks.explain: CT needs only data. Using the clean image that generated the noisy point gives an unbiased score estimate, and one Euler step with it lands on x + t_n z with the same noise draw. CD and progressive distillation both need a trained teacher.

blocks.question: A CD run uses an Euler teacher with N = 18 and reaches near-zero training loss, but one-step samples are slightly too smooth (under-dispersed). What change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer at the same settings
Use a higher-order teacher solver (Heun) or more grid points N
Increase the EMA decay to 0.99999
Set c_out(eps) to 0.5
blocks.explain: Zero CD loss means the model copies the teacher's one-step solver error, which accumulates along the chain (15% in the toy with Euler, N = 18). Heun or larger N shrinks it (5.5% with Heun, 0.2% with Heun and N = 80). Training longer cannot fix a biased target, and c_out(eps) must stay 0.

lessons.title: One-step and two-step sampling, and what the steps buy

blocks.md: One-step sampling is $x = f_\theta(x_T, T)$ with $x_T \sim N(0, T^2)$. Consistency models can also trade compute for quality. **Multistep consistency sampling** (Algorithm 1 in Song et al.) alternates denoising and noise injection: after the first jump, add fresh noise to bring the sample back to a chosen time $\tau$, then jump to the origin again.

blocks.tex: x \leftarrow f_\theta(x_T, T); \quad \hat{x}_{\tau} = x + \sqrt{\tau^2 - \epsilon^2}\, z; \quad x \leftarrow f_\theta(\hat{x}_{\tau}, \tau), \qquad z \sim N(0, I)
blocks.caption: Two-step sampling. The noise scale $\sqrt{\tau^2-\epsilon^2}$ turns a sample at level $\epsilon$ into one at level $\tau$. More times $\tau_1 > \tau_2 > \dots$ give more steps.

blocks.title: Two-step sampling on the toy with the exact f
blocks.code:
x_T = T * randn()                 # T = 80
x = f(x_T, T)                     # step 1: jump to origin
tau = 2.0
z = randn()
x_hat = x + sqrt(tau**2 - eps**2) * z
x = f(x_hat, tau)                 # step 2
return x

scenes.caption: Draw noise at T = 80. Here x_T = 104, a 1.3-sigma draw.
One evaluation maps it to its trajectory's origin: 104 times 0.00625 = 0.65. This alone is a valid sample (1 NFE).
Re-noise to tau = 2 with z = -0.7: 0.65 + 2.0 x (-0.7) = -0.75. The sample now sits on a different trajectory.
Jump again: -0.75 times 0.2425 = -0.1819. With an exact f both outputs are equally valid samples; with a learned f, step 2 can repair step 1's errors.

blocks.prompt: Take the zero-loss CD model from the last lesson (Euler teacher, N = 18), whose one-step samples have std 0.4230 instead of 0.5. Does adding a second step at some grid time tau fix it?
blocks.reveal: No. Computing every grid tau gives a two-step std between 0.4222 and 0.4230. In this toy the model's error is the same 15% shrink at every t above about 3 and is already about 13% at t = 1.09, so step 2 repeats the mistake. Multistep sampling helps only when the model is **more accurate at tau** than at T, which is typical for real networks because errors build up from the boundary outward.

blocks.title: Two-step std vs tau (hypothetical: step 1 biased, exact at tau)

scenes.caption: Simplified scenario: the first jump has the 15% shrink of the CD Euler model (std 0.4230) but the model is exact at tau. Re-noising to a tiny tau barely helps: 0.4263 at tau = 0.1.

Larger tau injects enough fresh noise to wash out step 1's error: 0.4958 at tau = 2, 0.4993 at tau = 5. Too large a tau, though, hands the hard high-noise jump back to the model; Song et al. pick tau by a ternary search on FID.
A 50-step ODE sampler runs the network 50 times in sequence. In the toy, 50 Euler steps still only reach std 0.4724 of the target 0.5.
A two-step consistency sampler: 2 NFE, 25 times fewer sequential evaluations.
One step: 1 NFE, a 50x saving. Each NFE costs about the same, since the consistency model reuses the diffusion architecture.

blocks.md: On real images the savings come with a quality gap. Song et al. report FID (Frechet Inception Distance, lower is better) for CD with LPIPS: **3.55** in 1 step and **2.93** in 2 steps on CIFAR-10, against 2.04 for the EDM sampler at 35 NFE. On ImageNet 64x64, CD gets **6.20** and **4.70**, against 2.44 for EDM at 79 NFE. The same multistep procedure also gives zero-shot editing (inpainting, colorization, super-resolution) without task-specific training.

blocks.question: Your 1-step consistency model makes slightly wrong images, mostly in coarse structure. Which second-step tau is the better first guess?
options: A moderate tau, large enough that fresh noise covers the coarse errors but well below T
tau = eps, so the second step changes nothing
tau = T, to restart from pure noise
No tau can help; use a 50-step ODE sampler
blocks.explain: In the hypothetical toy run, tau = 0.1 barely helped (0.4263) while tau = 2 recovered 0.4958. Fresh noise must be big enough to hide step 1's errors, but tau = T throws away step 1 and repeats the same hard jump. tau = eps adds no noise, so f returns its input.

blocks.question: The toy's CD Euler model gets no benefit from a second step, while real CD models improve from FID 3.55 to 2.93 on CIFAR-10. What explains the difference?
options: Real models use stochastic ODE solvers
The toy uses the wrong noise scale in re-noising
The toy's error is a uniform scale bias at all high t, while real networks are more accurate at moderate noise than at T
Two-step FID is measured with a different metric
blocks.explain: Re-noising to tau only helps if f is better at tau than at T. In the toy the CD error is about 13% to 15% at every t above 1, so step 2 repeats it. Both cases use the same deterministic Algorithm 1 and the same re-noising formula.

lessons.title: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers

blocks.md: **Improved consistency training (iCT).** Song and Dhariwal (2023) made CT beat CD without any teacher. The changes: remove the EMA from the teacher network; replace LPIPS (which shares ImageNet features with the FID evaluator) with the **Pseudo-Huber** loss $d(x, y) = \sqrt{\lVert x - y\rVert^2 + c^2} - c$; sample noise levels from a lognormal distribution (mean -1.1, std 2.0) instead of uniformly over the grid; and double $N$ at set intervals, from 10 up to 1280. Result, with the deeper iCT-deep network (standard iCT gets 2.83 and 2.46 on CIFAR-10): FID **2.51** in 1 step and **2.24** in 2 steps on CIFAR-10, **3.25** and **2.77** on ImageNet 64x64.

**Continuous-time CMs (sCM).** Taking $N \to \infty$ removes the discretization error from lesson 4 but needs Jacobian-vector products and was unstable. Lu and Song (2024) fixed this with TrigFlow, better time conditioning, tangent normalization and adaptive weighting, and scaled to 1.5B parameters on ImageNet 512x512. Two-step FIDs: **2.06** on CIFAR-10 (teacher 2.01), **1.48** on ImageNet 64x64 (teacher 1.33), **1.88** on ImageNet 512x512 (teacher 1.73), within 10% of the teacher.

blocks.title: CIFAR-10 FID (lower is better), as reported in the papers

scenes.caption: One step. Original CT (8.70) roughly matched progressive distillation (8.34); CD reached 3.55; iCT-deep 2.51 and sCT 2.85, all without adversarial training. EDM shown at 35 NFE as the multi-step reference (2.01 in the sCM paper).

Two steps. Everything improves: PD 5.58, CT 5.83, CD 2.93, iCT-deep 2.24, sCT 2.06, almost equal to the 35-step teacher. Numbers are from Song et al. 2023, Song and Dhariwal 2023, and Lu and Song 2024.

blocks.md: **Latent Consistency Models (LCM)**, Luo et al. 2023, apply CD in the latent space of Stable Diffusion. They distill a classifier-free-guided teacher by solving an *augmented* PF ODE that includes the guidance scale, and use a **skipping-step** target ($t_{n+k}$ to $t_n$ with $k = 20$) instead of adjacent steps on the 1000-step schedule. A 768x768 LCM for 2 to 4 steps took about 32 A100 GPU hours (4,000 training iterations).

blocks.title: Five ways to distill a diffusion teacher into few steps

scenes.caption: Progressive distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022): train a student so that 1 of its DDIM steps matches 2 teacher steps, then make the student the new teacher. 8192 steps down to 4, FID 3.0 on CIFAR-10 at 4 steps.
Consistency distillation needs no multi-stage chain: one model, trained on single-ODE-step pairs, samples in 1 step. LCM is the same idea in Stable Diffusion's latent space with guidance built in.

ADD (Sauer et al., 2023): the student gets a score distillation loss from a frozen teacher plus a hinge GAN loss from a discriminator on frozen ViT features. SDXL-Turbo is SDXL distilled with ADD for 1 to 4 steps.

DMD (Yin et al., 2023): minimize an approximate KL between generator and data distributions, whose gradient is the difference of a real score and a learned fake score, plus a regression loss to teacher outputs.
Consistency training is the one route here that needs no teacher at all, so its quality is not capped by one.

blocks.md: Reported results for the non-consistency methods: DMD reaches FID 2.62 on ImageNet 64x64 in one step and 11.49 on zero-shot COCO-30k, generating 512x512 images at 20 FPS with FP16 (90 ms per image vs 2590 ms for Stable Diffusion in their comparison). The ADD paper reports that ADD-XL beats LCM-XL and GAN baselines in one step in user studies and matches its SDXL teacher at four steps.

Failure modes and costs: distillation (CD, LCM, PD) is capped by the teacher's quality. Adversarial losses (ADD) bring GAN training complexity. The sCM paper notes that variational score distillation methods such as DMD can produce overly smooth samples with limited diversity. Continuous-time CM training was unstable until sCM's fixes. And 1-step quality still trails the multi-step teacher.

Consistency models learn the end of the ODE trajectory, not its slope. The boundary condition anchors the chain at the data; adjacent-time agreement (from a teacher's ODE step or from the data itself) propagates it to high noise; extra steps re-noise and jump again to trade compute for quality.

blocks.question: You need a one-step text-to-image model and have no budget for training a new diffusion model, but you do have a strong pretrained latent diffusion model with classifier-free guidance. Which approach fits best?
options: Latent consistency distillation (LCM) or adversarial diffusion distillation from that model
Consistency training from scratch on pixels
Progressive distillation from 8192 steps in pixel space
Plain L2 regression from noise to random images
blocks.explain: LCM and ADD both start from an existing latent diffusion teacher and target 1 to 4 steps; LCM distills the guided ODE directly (about 32 A100 hours for its 768x768 model). CT from scratch means training a new model; PD takes many halving stages; noise-to-random-image regression learns the mean.

blocks.question: Why did Song and Dhariwal replace LPIPS with a Pseudo-Huber loss in improved consistency training?
options: LPIPS cannot be differentiated
Pseudo-Huber is required for one-step sampling
LPIPS made training diverge on CIFAR-10
LPIPS uses ImageNet-trained features like the FID evaluator, which can inflate FID, and it costs an extra network pass
blocks.explain: The iCT paper names two downsides of LPIPS: possible evaluation bias because LPIPS and the Inception network behind FID both learned from ImageNet, and the compute of backpropagating through an extra network. Pseudo-Huber is robust to outliers and twice differentiable.
